details:
**Gleipnir**
The magical fetter the dwarves make to finally bind Fenrir. It looks like a thin silken ribbon but is made of six impossible things: the sound of a cat's footfall, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish, and the spittle of a bird. Because these were used up, they no longer exist in the world.

**Tyr loses his hand**
Fenrir suspects a trick and agrees to be bound with Gleipnir only if one of the gods puts a hand in his mouth as a pledge of good faith. Only Tyr, the god of war and law who had also been the only god brave enough to feed the wolf, does so. When Fenrir cannot break free, he bites off Tyr's right hand.

**Killing Odin at Ragnarok**
At Ragnarok, the end of the world in Norse myth, Fenrir breaks free of Gleipnir and swallows Odin, the chief of the gods. He advances with his lower jaw on the earth and his upper jaw against the sky, and flames burn from his eyes and nostrils.

**Vidar and the thick shoe**
Odin's son Vidar avenges his father by killing Fenrir. In Snorri's Prose Edda he steps on the wolf's lower jaw with a thick shoe made from all the leather scraps people have ever cut away, then tears the jaws apart; in the poem Voluspa he stabs the wolf in the heart.

**Skoll and Hati**
Fenrir's sons, born to a giantess in the forest Ironwood (Jarnvid). Skoll chases the sun, whose chariot is pulled by the horses Arvakr and Alsvidr, and Hati chases the moon (Mani). At Ragnarok they catch and swallow the sun and moon.

**Son of Loki and Angrboda**
Fenrir is one of three monstrous children of the trickster god Loki and the giantess Angrboda. His siblings are the world serpent Jormungandr and Hel, ruler of the dead. Prophecies said these children would bring disaster, so the gods brought the wolf to Asgard to keep watch on him.

**Laeding and Dromi**
The first two iron fetters the gods use on Fenrir as he grows alarmingly large. They present the binding as a test of strength, and he easily breaks both, which gave rise to sayings about "getting loose from Laeding" and "striking out of Dromi."

**River Van**
After he is bound, the gods jam a sword into Fenrir's mouth, with the hilt against his lower jaw and the point against his upper jaw, to keep him from biting. Drool and blood flowing from his mouth form the river Van, which gives him the name Vanagandr ("monster of the Van").

**Lyngvi, Amsvartnir, Gelgja, Gjoll, and Thviti**
Fenrir is bound on the island of Lyngvi in the lake Amsvartnir. The gods attach a cord called Gelgja to Gleipnir, thread it through a boulder called Gjoll, and fix it deep in the earth with a stone called Thviti.

**Gylfaginning (Prose Edda)**
Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda tells the full binding story in its Gylfaginning section, where the figure High explains it to the disguised king Gangleri. High says the gods did not simply kill Fenrir because they did not want to defile their sacred places with his blood.

**Thorwald's Cross and the Gosforth Cross**
Viking Age stone crosses with Fenrir imagery. Thorwald's Cross on the Isle of Man shows Odin, with a raven on his shoulder, being devoured by Fenrir, and the Gosforth Cross in Cumbria is usually read as showing Vidar confronting the wolf, scenes that may parallel Christian images of Satan's defeat.

**Alternate names: Fenrisulfr, Hrodvitnir, Vanagandr**
Fenrir is also called the Fenris wolf (Fenrisulfr), Hrodvitnir ("famous wolf"), and Vanagandr ("monster of the river Van"). Any of these may appear as accepted answers.
